teaser.en: A roadside weed with a long green whip of a flower spike, dotted each morning with a few small blue flowers.

summary.en: Mruwa is the blue porterweed, a low shrubby weed of open ground with small blue flowers on long, stiff spikes. Pakia lists it among the few plants the Digo identify by their flowers, because it is valued as an ornament.

about.en: Mruwa is a low, branching, somewhat woody herb, usually knee- to waist-high, with toothed, slightly rough leaves in opposite pairs. Its flowers come on long, thin green spikes that stand up like whips. Only a few flowers open at a time, small and bright blue to violet, set into the spike, and they last a single day.

where.en: Originally from tropical America, it is now a common weed of roadsides, compounds, farm edges and waste ground along the coast. It is also grown in gardens, and butterflies visit it constantly.

uses.en: Pakia records it among plants valued for ornament, alongside bougainvillea, yellow oleander and lantana.

culture.en: Digo people seldom use flowers to tell plants apart; Pakia found they mostly look at leaves. The exceptions are plants whose flowers matter to people, such as perfume plants and ornamentals, and Mruwa is one of them. The name itself appears linked to the Digo word ruwa (flower) and to maruwa, the beautifying decorations Pakia describes, but Pakia does not give its meaning.

names.en: Pakia records the Digo name Mruwa. In English it is blue porterweed or Jamaica vervain; its scientific name is Stachytarpheta jamaicensis. No Swahili name is given in the sources used here.

reason.en: Another introduced ornamental-turned-weed in the verbena family
Also identified by its ornamental flowers
Ornamental plant recognised by its flowers
